narrative:
The model predicted an 88% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, followed by your LSAT score, then your first-year class ranking. All three pushed the prediction strongly toward failure.

Your first-year and third-year grades both placed you in the bottom decile of your school. While the average student who is accepted sits around the middle of their class (roughly 6th decile), you ranked at the very bottom in both periods. These unusually low academic standings were the main reasons the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar. Your LSAT score of 23 also pulled the prediction downward; it is well below the 37-point average of accepted applicants and signaled weaker preparation for the exam.

Your family income, undergraduate GPA, full-time status, gender, and race played little or no role in this outcome, as the model focused on academic performance signals.

To improve your chances, you should retake the LSAT and aim for a substantially higher score, while also strengthening your academic record through additional coursework or a strong graduate program. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction. (218 words)
